# Survey Methods and Discovering Customer Preferences

Why direct survey questions can be misleading, and how tools like MaxDiff and conjoint analysis help marketers reveal what people actually value.

<p class="muted">MGTA 495: Marketing Analytics</p>



## Customers Say One Thing, Choose Another

<div class="grid2">
<div class="card">
<h2>What surveys ask</h2>
<p>"How important is price?"</p>
<p>"Would you buy this?"</p>
<p>"What would you pay?"</p>
</div>
<div class="card">
<h2>What marketers need</h2>
<p>Would they choose it?</p>
<p>What would they trade off?</p>
<p>At what price do they switch?</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="callout"><p><span class="highlight">Main idea:</span> Good marketing research does not just ask people what they want. It creates choices that reveal what people value.</p></div>

::: notes
The problem is not that customers are lying. The problem is that direct questions often ask people to predict future behavior in a situation with no real trade-offs.
:::

## Why Traditional Ratings Fail

<div class="grid3">
<div class="card">
<h2>Hypothetical Bias</h2>
<p class="small">No money is on the line.</p>
<p class="bad">Intentions get inflated.</p>
</div>
<div class="card">
<h2>Scale-Use Bias</h2>
<p class="small">One person's 8/10 is another person's 5/10.</p>
<p class="bad">Ratings are not comparable.</p>
</div>
<div class="card">
<h2>No Trade-Offs</h2>
<p class="small">People can say everything matters.</p>
<p class="bad">Nothing is prioritized.</p>
</div>
</div>

<br>

| Feature | Average Importance |
|---|---:|
| Lower price | 9.2 |
| Better quality | 9.1 |
| Faster delivery | 8.9 |
| Eco-friendly packaging | 8.7 |
| Premium design | 8.5 |

<p class="caption">This looks like data, but it does not tell the manager what to build first. Traditional rating questions often produce compressed results. Everything looks important. But if every feature is important, the survey has not helped the company make a decision.
</p>


## MaxDiff: Don't Rate Everything — Choose

MaxDiff asks respondents to pick the <span class="good">MOST</span> and <span class="bad">LEAST</span> important item from a small set.

<div class="grid2">
<div>
<div class="feature-card most"><p><span class="good">MOST</span>: Lower price</p></div>
<div class="feature-card"><p>Better battery life</p></div>
<div class="feature-card"><p>Better camera</p></div>
<div class="feature-card least"><p><span class="bad">LEAST</span>: Brand reputation</p></div>
</div>
<div class="card">
<h2>Why it works</h2>
<ul>
<li>Forces trade-offs</li>
<li>Avoids scale-use bias</li>
<li>Prevents "everything is important"</li>
<li>Creates a clear ranking</li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>

::: notes
MaxDiff is useful when marketers have a long list of features, claims, benefits, or messages. Instead of asking people to rate each item, it forces prioritization.
:::

## Conjoint: Make the Survey Feel Like Shopping

Conjoint shows people realistic product bundles and asks them to choose.

<div class="grid2">
<div class="card">
<h3>Option A</h3>
<p><strong>$49/month</strong></p>
<p>Fast delivery</p>
<p>Basic support</p>
<p>Standard packaging</p>
</div>
<div class="card">
<h3>Option B</h3>
<p><strong>$59/month</strong></p>
<p>Standard delivery</p>
<p>Premium support</p>
<p>Eco-friendly packaging</p>
</div>
</div>

<p class="arrow">Choice data -> Part-worths -> Willingness to pay -> Market share</p>

::: notes
Conjoint goes beyond MaxDiff because it studies bundles of attributes. It lets marketers estimate how much people value each feature, how sensitive they are to price, and how a new product might perform in the market.
:::

## The Statistical Engine: MNL + MLE

<div class="grid2">
<div class="card">
<h3>Multinomial Logit</h3>
<p class="small">Turns product features into choice probabilities.</p>
<p class="small">Higher utility -> higher probability of being chosen.</p>
</div>
<div class="card">
<h3>Maximum Likelihood</h3>
<p class="small">Finds the parameters that make the observed choices most likely.</p>
<p class="small">This is how we estimate preferences from choices.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="callout">
<p>Instead of asking, <span class="bad">"What do you want?"</span></p>
<p>We ask, <span class="good">"Which option did you choose?"</span></p>
</div>

::: notes
The model behind this is the multinomial logit model. Each product has utility based on its features and price. MLE estimates the feature values that best explain the choices people made.
:::

## What Marketers Can Do With This

<div class="grid2">
<div class="card">
<h3>Product decisions</h3>
<ul>
<li>Which features matter?</li>
<li>Which bundle should we launch?</li>
<li>Which segment values what?</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="card">
<h3>Pricing decisions</h3>
<ul>
<li>How price-sensitive are customers?</li>
<li>What is willingness to pay?</li>
<li>What price maximizes revenue?</li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>

<br>

<div class="card"><h3>Market simulation</h3><p>Change a feature, change a price, add a competitor, and recompute predicted market shares.</p></div>

::: notes
This is the practical value of conjoint. Once we have the model, we can simulate choices for products that do not even exist yet.
:::

## One More Warning: Behavior Can Mislead Too

<div class="grid2">
<div class="card">
<h3>Naive conclusion</h3>
<p>Customers who got the email spent more.</p>
<p class="bad">So the email caused higher spending.</p>
</div>
<div class="card">
<h3>Better question</h3>
<p>Were those customers already more likely to spend?</p>
<p class="good">Random assignment fixes selection bias.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="callout"><p>Marketing analytics is not just about more data. It is about better research design.</p></div>

::: notes
This connects to causal inference. Even real behavioral data can be misleading if the treated group was already different. That is why experiments and random assignment are so valuable.
:::

## The Big Takeaway

<div class="grid2">
<div class="card">
<h3 class="bad">Weak research</h3>
<p>Ask direct questions</p>
<p>Get easy answers</p>
<p>Miss trade-offs</p>
</div>
<div class="card">
<h3 class="good">Strong research</h3>
<p>Create realistic choices</p>
<p>Estimate preferences</p>
<p>Simulate better decisions</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="callout">
<p class="big">Good marketers do not just ask customers what they want.</p>
<p class="big">They design research that reveals what customers are willing to choose.</p>
</div>

::: notes
End with the main message. The course tools all point in the same direction: move away from surface-level answers and toward designs that reveal preferences through choices.
:::

## Optional 3-Minute Script

<p class="small">Today I'm talking about why asking customers what they want often does not work. Customers can describe past behavior, but they are much less reliable at predicting what they will buy in the future.</p>

<p class="small">Traditional surveys fail because they create bias. People overstate intentions, answer in socially desirable ways, and use scales differently. Most importantly, they avoid trade-offs.</p>

<p class="small">MaxDiff improves this by forcing people to choose the most and least important item. Conjoint goes further by making the survey feel like shopping. Respondents choose between product bundles, and the model estimates which features and prices drove those choices.</p>

<p class="small">The takeaway is simple: direct questions often produce unreliable answers, but choice-based methods reveal what customers actually value.</p>
